simple: a tiny electrical switch with no moving parts, turned on and off by a voltage.
analogy: a tap in the building's plumbing, opened by a small control valve.
precise: a semiconductor device in which the voltage on one terminal, the gate, controls the current between two other terminals; in digital logic it is used as an on/off switch, a voltage-controlled switch. (A MOS transistor also has a fourth terminal, the body, which this course does not use.)
source: D2 ch.1 summary, D8 §6.1, D7 L3 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the three wires of a transistor: one that controls it, and two that are joined when it is on.
analogy: the thin control pipe (gate), and the two ends of the big pipe through the tap (source and drain).
precise: in a MOS transistor the gate terminal controls whether a conducting channel forms between the source and drain terminals. The word "gate" also names a whole logic circuit (F1-10); the context says which one is meant.
source: D7 L3 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the two kinds of transistor switch: nMOS turns on when its gate is 1, pMOS turns on when its gate is 0.
analogy: two kinds of tap: one opens when the control pipe has pressure, the other opens when it has none.
precise: n-channel and p-channel metal-oxide-semiconductor field-effect transistors; in the ideal-switch model of digital logic, an nMOS conducts when its gate is at logic 1 and a pMOS conducts when its gate is at logic 0.
source: D2 ch.1 summary, D7 L1, R2 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a way of building logic where every output has pMOS switches to the supply and nMOS switches to ground.
analogy: each sink has one set of taps from the roof tank and a matching set of taps to the drain, and only one set is open at a time.
precise: complementary MOS: logic built from a pull-up network of pMOS transistors and a complementary pull-down network of nMOS transistors, so that for every input exactly one network conducts.
source: D7 L1, D8 §6.2 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the switches that connect the output to 1 (pull-up) or to 0 (pull-down).
analogy: the taps between the sink and the roof tank (pull-up), and between the sink and the drain (pull-down).
precise: in a CMOS gate, the pull-up network joins the output to the supply rail and the pull-down network joins it to ground; their switch patterns are complements of each other.
source: D7 L1, D8 §6.2 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit whose output is the opposite of its input.
analogy: a sink that fills when the control pipe is empty and drains when it has pressure.
precise: the logic function y = NOT a; in CMOS, one pMOS pull-up and one nMOS pull-down with their gates joined to the input.
source: D7 L1, R2 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: floating means the output is connected to nothing; a short means it is connected to 1 and 0 at the same time.
analogy: a sink with every tap shut, so nobody can say how full it is; or a sink with the roof tank and the drain both open, so water rushes straight through.
precise: Verilog writes a floating (high-impedance) value as z and an unknown value, such as two strong drivers in conflict, as x; in a real circuit a short between supply and ground draws a large current.
source: D5, R3, D8 §6.2 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a language for writing down a circuit as text: its parts and the wires between them.
analogy: the written plan of the building's pipes, which a practice kitchen can follow exactly.
precise: a computer language whose descriptions specify the structure and behaviour of digital hardware so that tools can simulate it or turn it into gates; Verilog is the HDL used in this course.
source: D1 §1.1.4, D9 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a program that pretends to be a circuit; a testbench is the extra code that tries inputs and checks outputs.
analogy: a practice kitchen where you test a recipe before the real dinner, and a tasting checklist.
precise: a simulator computes the values of the wires of a circuit description over time; a testbench is a description that applies input values (test vectors) to the design under test and compares its outputs with expected values.
source: D1 §1.1.4–1.1.5 of F1-09 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a small circuit that computes one logic function, such as NOT or AND, from its inputs.
analogy: one sink with its own set of taps, whose fill level answers one yes/no question.
precise: an electronic circuit implementing a Boolean function of one or more binary inputs; in CMOS, a pull-up and a pull-down network of transistors. "Gate" also names one terminal of a transistor (F1-09).
source: D1 §1.1.2, D8 §6.2 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: "not and": the output is 0 only when all inputs are 1.
analogy: Kenji's sink: it drains only when both drain taps are open.
precise: the Boolean function y = NOT (a AND b); in CMOS, two nMOS in series to ground and two pMOS in parallel to the supply.
source: D8 §6.3–6.4, D7 L1, R1 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: "not or": the output is 1 only when all inputs are 0.
analogy: a sink with two drain taps side by side and two roof taps one after the other.
precise: the Boolean function y = NOT (a OR b); in CMOS, two nMOS in parallel to ground and two pMOS in series to the supply.
source: D8 §6.3–6.4, R1 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: series means one after another, so all must be on; parallel means side by side, so any one is enough.
analogy: two taps on one pipe, one after the other, or two pipes joined side by side.
precise: switches in series conduct only if every switch conducts (an AND of their conditions); switches in parallel conduct if at least one conducts (an OR).
source: D7 L1, D3 ch.6, D8 §6.2 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the standard drawing for each kind of gate, with inputs on the left and the output on the right.
analogy: the little picture on a kitchen door that tells you what happens in that room.
precise: a schematic shape: a triangle for a buffer, a D shape for AND, a curved shield for OR; a small circle (bubble) on an output or input means inversion.
source: D1 §1.1.2, Fig. 1.3 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: trying every possible input and checking every output.
analogy: tasting every dish on the menu, not only the favourites.
precise: a test whose vectors cover all 2n combinations of n binary inputs; for small combinational circuits this proves the circuit matches its truth table.
source: D1 §1.1.1, §1.1.4, W1 of F1-10 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a set of gates is complete if you can build every logic function from it; a gate that is complete on its own is called universal.
analogy: Zofia's one knife that can do every kitchen job, with enough moves.
precise: a set of Boolean operations is functionally complete if every Boolean function can be expressed using only operations from the set; {NAND} and {NOR} are each functionally complete.
source: D1 §1.1.1, §1.4, D8 §7.5 of F1-11 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the opposite of XOR: 1 when the inputs are equal.
analogy: a "same?" checker for two switches.
precise: y = NOT (a XOR b); truth table 1, 0, 0, 1.
source: W1 of F1-11 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: describing a circuit by listing its parts and how they are wired, not by writing a formula.
analogy: a floor plan showing every pipe and tap, instead of a sentence saying "the sink fills when…".
precise: an HDL description built from instances of gates or modules connected by named wires; the opposite style, describing what the output should be, is called behavioural.
source: D1 §1.1.4, D2 §4.3 of F1-11 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a program that turns a circuit description into a list of gates.
analogy: a head chef who reads "make soup for twelve" and writes the exact steps and tools.
precise: software that translates an HDL description into a netlist of cells from a target library (here, NAND and NOT cells), usually trying to reduce some cost.
source: D6 help synth, abc, D7 L2 of F1-11 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the list of every gate in a circuit and the wires that join them.
analogy: the plumber's parts list with every pipe connection written down.
precise: a description of a circuit as instances (cells) and the nets (wires) connecting their pins.
source: D7 L2, D6 help stat of F1-11 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit whose outputs depend only on its inputs right now, with no memory.
analogy: the pass: what goes through depends only on the plates and the ticket in front of Mateo, not on yesterday's orders.
precise: a digital circuit without feedback or storage, whose outputs are a Boolean function of its current inputs (after the outputs settle, F1-15). Circuits with memory are sequential (HW201).
source: D2 ch.2 summary, D8 §7.7 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit that chooses one of several inputs and passes it to the output.
analogy: Mateo sliding one station's plate through the hatch.
precise: a combinational circuit with 2n data inputs, n select inputs and one output, whose output equals the data input whose index is the binary number on the select inputs.
source: D1 §1.2.2, §1.2.4, D8 §7.8.1 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the input that says which choice to make, written as a binary number.
analogy: the order number on the ticket.
precise: the control inputs of a multiplexer or decoder; with n select bits there are 2n choices.
source: D1 §1.2.4, D8 §7.8.1 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit that turns a binary number into one active line out of many.
analogy: the ticket board lighting exactly one station lamp.
precise: a combinational circuit with n inputs and 2n outputs, of which exactly the output whose index equals the input number is 1 (when enabled).
source: D8 §7.8.3.1 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: an on/off input that lets a circuit work or keeps all its outputs off.
analogy: the main switch of the ticket board: when it is off, no lamp lights.
precise: an input that, when inactive, forces a decoder's outputs to their inactive value (here 0) regardless of the other inputs.
source: W1, R1 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a group of wires where exactly one is 1.
analogy: one lit lamp on the ticket board.
precise: an encoding in which exactly one bit of a group is 1; a decoder's outputs are one-hot when enabled.
source: D8 §7.8.3.1 of F1-12 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: when you add one column, the sum bit is the digit you write down and the carry bit is what you pass to the next column.
analogy: Hana's board after the flip (sum) and the runner's token (carry).
precise: for inputs whose total in one column is T (0 to 3), the sum bit is T mod 2 and the carry bit is T div 2 (integer division).
source: W1, D1 §2.2.1, D3 ch.14 of F1-13 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit that adds two bits and gives a sum bit and a carry bit.
analogy: one board with no runner arriving.
precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b and outputs s = a XOR b and c = a AND b, so that 2c + s = a + b.
source: D1 §2.3, D3 ch.14, R1 of F1-13 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a circuit that adds three bits: two digits and a carry coming in.
analogy: a board whose cook also takes the runner's token.
precise: a combinational circuit with inputs a, b, cin and outputs s = a XOR b XOR cin and cout = (a AND b) OR (cin AND (a XOR b)), so that 2·cout + s = a + b + cin.
source: D1 §2.2.1, D3 ch.14, R1 of F1-13 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the carry arriving from the column to the right, and the carry leaving to the column to the left.
analogy: the token the runner brings, and the token sent on.
precise: the carry input and carry output of a full adder; chaining cout of one bit to cin of the next makes a multi-bit adder (F1-14).
source: D1 §2.3, D3 ch.14 of F1-13 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: how many bits Verilog uses to work out an expression.
analogy: a board that only has room for one digit: a total of 3 is written as 1 and the rest is lost.
precise: Verilog sizes an expression from its operands and its context; adding three 1-bit values in a 1-bit context keeps only the low bit. The run width_demo shows it.
source: D5, R3 of F1-13 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a multi-bit adder made by chaining full adders, each passing its carry to the next.
analogy: the row of counting boards, with the runner's token travelling from right to left.
precise: an N-bit adder of N full adders in which the carry out of bit i is the carry in of bit i + 1; the carry may have to pass ("ripple") through every bit.
source: D1 §2.3, D3 ch.14, R1 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the part of a processor that does arithmetic and logic on two numbers, choosing the operation from a code.
analogy: Ines's prep station with its tools and the selector dial.
precise: a combinational circuit with two N-bit operands, an operation code (opcode) and an N-bit result plus status flags; it computes several functions and selects one with a multiplexer.
source: D1 §2.2.2, D8 §12.1.1 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a small binary number that says which operation the ALU should do.
analogy: the dial position on Ines's station.
precise: the select input of the ALU's result multiplexer and of any operation-specific logic; this chapter's ALU uses a 3-bit code with eight operations.
source: W1 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: extra one-bit outputs that report facts about the result: is it zero, is it negative, did the addition carry out, did it overflow?
analogy: the four lamps on the station's panel.
precise: Z = 1 when every result bit is 0; N = the top bit of the result (its sign in two's complement); C = the carry out of the top bit for ADD and SUB; V = 1 when a signed (two's complement) ADD or SUB gives a result outside the range of N bits.
source: D1 §2.2.2, D8 §3.2.1.2, R3 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the true answer is too big or too small to fit, so the bits show a wrong signed number.
analogy: a four-board row asked to show a count that needs five boards, read as a signed count.
precise: in N-bit two's complement, the representable range is −2N−1 to 2N−1 − 1; a signed sum outside that range overflows; this happens exactly when the carry into the top bit differs from the carry out of it.
source: D8 §3.2.1.2, W1, R3, R4 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a second, simpler description of what the answer should be, used to check the circuit.
analogy: the head chef's recipe card that the tasting checks against.
precise: an independent implementation of the specification (here, integer arithmetic in the testbench) whose outputs are compared with the design under test for every applied vector.
source: D1 §1.1.4 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: test inputs that look random but come from a formula, so the same list appears every run.
analogy: a tasting list drawn by lottery, but from a lottery whose draw can be repeated exactly.
precise: inputs produced by a deterministic generator from a fixed seed; used when exhaustive testing is too large; the run is repeatable because the seed is fixed.
source: D5, R4 of F1-14 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the time from an input changing to the output reaching its new, final value.
analogy: the time between an order arriving and the plate being finished on the counter.
precise: the maximum time from a change at a circuit's input until its output is stable at the new value; for a path through several gates it is the sum of the gate delays along the path.
source: D8 §6.4, §7.7 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the shortest time before an output can start to change after an input changes.
analogy: how soon the first cook can touch the plate after the order arrives.
precise: the minimum time from an input change until any output begins to change; together with the propagation delay it bounds when an output may be changing.
source: D8 §6.4, §7.7 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: the slowest route from any input to any output.
analogy: the order that has to visit every station in the row.
precise: the path through a combinational circuit with the largest sum of gate delays; it sets the circuit's propagation delay.
source: D8 §7.7, §12.2.2 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: to stop changing and show the final answer.
analogy: the moment the last cook puts down the spoon.
precise: a combinational output has settled when, after an input change, no further change will happen until the inputs change again; before that it may show wrong intermediate values.
source: W1, R2 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a short wrong pulse on an output that should not have changed.
analogy: a plate that briefly disappears from the counter while two cooks swap places, then comes back.
precise: an unwanted transient on a combinational output caused by different path delays, for example a momentary 0 on an output whose correct value stays 1.
source: D8 §7.7, §7.7.1, R3 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)

simple: a picture of signals changing over time, one row per signal.
analogy: the kitchen's order log with a time for every step.
precise: a plot of signal values against time; high and low levels for single bits, and labelled segments for multi-bit values (buses).
source: D7 L11, R2 of F1-15 (verified 2026-10-10; see the chapter's Sources and dossier)
